#6474. Christopher Bailey on His Post-Burberry Reinvention at the Historic Burleigh Pottery

In Stoke-on-Trent one balmy day this summer, a Victorian world unfurled at an earthenware manufacturer I had come to visit. Middleport Pottery, the Grade II*-listed home of Burleigh Pottery, built in 1888, is seemingly unchanged since then, as women mill around its cobbled walkways wearing patched crinoline skirts and poke bonnets, and men model timeworn top hats and darned waistcoats. An embarrassment of wooden stalls with a panoply of foodstuffs, including a rather fly-friendly table of fish, moulder in the midday sun, while an assortment of mismatched Victorian underwear hangs to dry.

The pottery has surrendered its photogenic aspects to a TV production crew, intent on making it an authentic, bustling 19th-century scene, but Burleigh’s story began about 40 years before this state-of-the-art manufactory was completed, in 1851, as Hulme & Booth. When William Leigh and Frederick Rathbone Burgess took over in 1862, it became known as Burgess & Leigh, and the abbreviated name, Burleigh, was adopted in 1903.

Bowls come out of the dipping house before their final firing.

In 2010, it was acquired by British ceramics company Denby and, that same year, the Prince’s Regeneration Trust stepped in with a substantial £9 million sum to purchase and save the building from severe disrepair. The Prince of Wales (now King Charles III) visited the site in 2013, returning five more times. Since then, its history has been mixed, until it was recently threatened with closure. Sixty-two jobs at risk; the only pottery in the world to use underglaze tissue printing, whereby potters apply designs to vessels using tracing paper, its lengths almost hemming them in like a Victorian laundry. (Such is the commitment to this 1750s-born craft that one woman has an elaborate web of tattoos—taken from a Burleigh design—on her calves, which peeks out of her shorts as she works.)

In 2018, Christopher Bailey had given up his roles of chief creative officer and president of Burberry, where he had transformed the brand since 2001 (after stints at Gucci with Tom Ford, and Donna Karan), to focus on his all-enveloping private life. “I had always hoped to have children but never actually—certainly growing up as a young gay man in quite a tough part of Yorkshire—thought that would even be within the realms of possibility,” says Halifax-born Bailey, who is now based in Oxfordshire. “And then [I was] able to have a family and get married to a man [actor Simon Woods] and go on my Burberry adventure and all these things, these amazing, happy accidents.” Giving up his high-powered job gave him time to lavish on his girls, Iris and Nell, now in their pre-teens.

Biscuit selector Shirley inspects, brushes, and tings each piece.

One spring Sunday afternoon this year, after his husband had departed for France to shoot a film for several weeks, Bailey was walking his dog Beckett with his children. He received a phone call from a friend, who told him the news that Denby had entered administration. “I knew the product,” says Bailey. “And I said, ‘I don’t have an emotional affinity with Denby. But let me look into it because maybe there’s more to it than I understand.’ I finished the walk and couldn’t stop thinking about it… I realized that Denby was the parent company for Burleigh. I’ve always loved Burleigh.” (At the age of 17, Bailey had worked for a wedding dress company in Hebden Bridge, just outside Halifax, “in one of those extraordinary buildings”—so the industrial Victorian style of the 1880s Burleigh workshop was familiar to him.) By June, it was announced that Bailey had acquired the company, alongside a small group of private investors.

Jemma Baskeyfield, the brand marketing manager, retail manager, and company historian who has been at the firm for 26 years, was practically the first person Bailey met at Burleigh. She educated him about every facet of the company and the specific language of pottery making: the fettler, the jolly, the monkey’s tail, the sherd-ruck, the potter’s rot. “I think you were cleaning everything up as well, after everyone had gone,” remembers Bailey. “We do wear a few hats,” says Baskeyfield.

Christopher Bailey at his new workplace, Middleport Pottery in Stoke-on-Trent.

“Feeling the weight of a 175-year-old company and giving its best face to Christopher when he first visited was a huge responsibility. I gave it a decent stab,” she continues.

“You did more than that,” replies Bailey. “You made me fall completely in love. I called Simon and said, ‘We’re putting our pension into a little pottery in Staffordshire.’”

“I just felt good here. I felt quite nurtured,” he says of his inauguration into the company, as we wander through its endless ateliers. “I grew up in a very post-industrial, historically thriving textile town, and the majority of businesses there were on their last legs.” Here, every employee has a unique skill, something that can only be done by hand. “Once I heard the most beautiful sound, and I was told, ‘Shirley’s listening to the pings.’ She tings the piece she’s working on with another piece of pottery and can tell if there’s any air trapped in it.”

In a ground floor room is a Dickensian treasure trove of white plaster molds, housed on floor-to-ceiling shelving. “Magical,” is how Bailey describes it. “I need to get everything digitized,” he says with a sigh. Archiving is a substantial future project. “We make things, but there’s never been a pause to say, ‘What do we have? And how can we make sure that we’re protecting things and using things?’ Because right now, it’s quite difficult to… find things. I’ve had quite a few projects where I just need to know, do we have this kind of a shape? This kind of a size? This kind of a vessel? And two days later, I’m still searching for it.”

The Arden design on this teacup has been part of Burleigh collections for more than 100 years.

They have a collection of more than 25,000 master molds; a complete archive of engravings, which number more than 5,000, from across the company’s history; and all of the original engraved cylinders. “So, basically, the tissue transfer process is where you get a copper cylinder, you hand-draw the design and then engrave it with a hammer and tools. So you’ve got two rollers and you put tissue through it, along with an ink,” Bailey explains, emphasizing that the only thing that doesn’t come from within 100 miles is the tobacco tissue—the right consistency and weight—from France. “Then these very skilled people cut the printed tissue out, and they literally wrap the vessel, whatever it is, a teapot, a cup, a plate. And with a brush, they push the ink into what’s called biscuit, where the pot has gone through the kiln one time. The paper gets washed off leaving the print, which gets glazed and goes for another firing in the kiln. And that kind of firing changes the color.”

Bailey had always thought that if he decided to have “another phase of life,” it would be in a big, tech-based—“because I love technology”—fashion company. “And so it’s quite funny that the thing that actually made my heart sing is practically AI-proof, because it can’t be replicated by technology.” He has plans to make the product—which is sought after by Soho House, William Morris gallery, and Ralph Lauren—more eclectic. “We’re very botanical, we’re very flowers and leaves. How can that kind of evolve? The patterns and colors, I think, can continue to have creativity instilled in them.”

Once fired, items are stored in the biscuit warehouse.

There are similarities between the worlds of fashion and pottery. “I remember, when I was 16, taking a coach to Paris from Halifax because I wanted to get into the Mugler and Chanel shows,” Bailey recalls. “I was a 16-year-old snotty-nosed kid, not dressed the way that you should be dressed for that kind of audience. I was very naïve, but I found it a magical world. And the way it’s changed, that kind of industrialization of fashion—it’s just what’s happened in much of the ceramics industry.”

At Burleigh, the hand still sings. “I really feel, in some ways, it’s this extraordinary 175-year-old start-up,” says Bailey, “and I’m enjoying that. I’m enjoying rolling up my sleeves. At Burberry, it was just an enormous responsibility. And I feel that here, but actually, I’m starting at the bottom. My whole mantra is: preserve this, but just make sure that we put in really good systems underneath.”

Hailing from a working-class background, Bailey views his hard work as a badge of honor. “My parents were grafters and they instilled that in me,” he explains. “But my girls… I stopped working when they were very young. I felt concerned that they were seeing me always being available and my purpose was solely to look after them and our life and our family. Parenting is an incredible skill and something that I’m very much learning. But professionally, I wasn’t really doing anything. And so I feel really excited and kind of slightly relieved that the girls are seeing me doing something that I’m loving. I’m not being paid for it, but that’s OK. One day it might happen.”

“I’m working very late at night and very early in the morning—on every facet. The operational side, the team side, the where-to-invest side, the rebuilding a website, the creative voice. I’m feeling energized by it.” He looks around the pottery’s workshops. “The team is really generous,” he adds. “They’re very proud. And so many of the amazing people here, their grandparents and parents were in the potteries. And so it’s not so much a job or a vocation. It is a culture.”

At the end of the day, when he considers the Burleigh world, “I feel joyful,” says Bailey.

#6473. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6472. GQ’s Best Gifts for Men 2026: 70+ Editor-Approved Presents

There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men. Stuff worth giving? That's another story. Fortunately, finding stuff worth giving is a salaried position around here. The results of that extensive retail research are all here: a carefully considered mix of great clothes, clever gadgets, handsome home goods, and a few things he probably wouldn't think to buy himself. We keep this guide updated throughout the year, so below you'll find our latest favorites alongside a few perennial heaters, all handpicked to make your gift-giving duties a little easier.

Still got names to cross off your list? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for a steady supply of good ideas.

This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.

Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe. This weathered slub denim version is a handsome example, and something he'll wear for years to come.

Few knits occupy a place in the menswear pantheon quite like J.Crew's rollneck sweater. With its relaxed weave and raglan sleeves, it's an enduring heater that makes for an easy gift.

What makes Morjas' Belgian loafer so irresistible to those who've had the good fortune to wear it is just how comfortable it is. Doesn't hurt that it's also clean, understated, and versatile as all get-out.

Maple's Orbit bracelet is a great little way to add a fleck of personality to an otherwise understated fit. And if this design is a little too out-there for his taste, you may have to look elsewhere entirely. That's kind of Maple's whole thing.

Smaller, thinner cases are great, and the Timex Marlin is a stone-cold minimalist classic in that world. But it also sells out, so allow us to recommend another, newer Timex gem: the Marlin Jet Titanium. He'll love that it's an automatic, too.

Patagonia's Snap-T is an icon, and this new Re-Tool Air version gives it a fresh spin with an exclusive Polartec fleece that's remarkably lightweight, wonderfully warm, and made from 100% recycled polyester.

This merino wool crewneck from Arc'teryx is lightweight, great at regulating temperature, and just as good worn on its own as it is layered under a sweater or jacket. A go-to layering piece for just about any wardrobe.

If you ask us, the Moon Shoe is one of the Swoosh's best releases of the year. A perfectly retro, low-profile runner with a refreshingly affordable price tag.

A great hoodie is essential, and Reigning Champ nails fit-meets-function better than most, with an aesthetic inspired by old-school athletic training gear. This one is cut from the brand’s signature midweight terry, which is soft and substantial without feeling bulky.

A man can never have enough flannels. Filson's Rangeland is made from brushed 5.5-ounce cotton, and we're partial to the red and gray plaid.

Massachusetts-based Steele Canvas has been making sturdy canvas goods for generations, and its Everyday Tote is exactly the sort of gift they'll most definitely get some use out of.

When we think of field watches, we think of Hamilton. This no-nonsense mechanical number is hard to beat in the category, and you could spend a lot more on a lot less.

A good pair of cowboy boots can do wonders for a fit, and Tecovas' Warren makes a strong case for adding a little yee-haw to the rotation. With classic flame stitching and a sharp cutter toe, they're more versatile than you might think.

3sixteen's asymmetrical fleece is freaky, but not too freaky, with a wide boatneck, an off-center zipper at the neck, and an oversized pocket with a zip closure. There's a lot going on, but the proportions are spot-on.

Some of the best stuff Miansai makes is low-key its bead and stone jewelry. The Avi necklace is a welcome change of pace from the usual gold and silver.

John Smedley has been making knitwear in England for more than 200 years, and there's a reason it's still considered some of the best in the biz. This wool polo might look simple, but the quality of the knit, the fit, and the finishing make it something special.

OrSlow's 105 jeans have a classic straight leg and medium rise, with the kind of easy, timeless fit that never goes out of style. A very good upgrade for anyone whose denim rotation could use a little love.

Yes, it costs a pretty penny. But it also might be one of the coolest scarves we’ve ever seen: so robust you can wrap it around yourself a few times like a sweater, at which point the price starts to make more sense. Oh, and it’s Burberry.

Movado's iconic Museum Watch has been a masterclass in minimalism since 1947, with a Bauhaus-inspired dial that's blank save for a single dot at 12 o'clock. A remarkably sleek timepiece, especially at this price.

Some days call for a full wallet, others for just the essentials. Coach's 3-in-1 gives him both, with a removable ID insert that works just as well on its own when he wants to travel a little lighter.

For the record, we're all for giving socks as presents, provided they're of the same caliber as those from Japan's Rototo.

Quince is one of our first stops for affordable cashmere, but its merino wool offerings ain't too shabby either. Take this sweater, which it done up in cable-knit for a little somethin' somethin'.

Blundstone introduced its Heritage boot this year, a decidedly more upscale take on the brand's beloved Chelsea. Handmade from premium leather, it's also finished with a Goodyear welt that allows it to be resoled for years to come.

Come for the three iconic Byredo scents, which you can spritz according to whatever the mood calls for. Stay for the handsome leather case, which is almost reason enough to gift the set on its own.

Plenty of dopp kits come in sleek leather (no shade), and plenty of designer versions cost a small fortune (some shade). But most guys just want something that looks good and can take a beating on the road. Filson knows how to do that.

Bar soaps have officially entered the elevated grooming arena, with better ingredients and better scents. Made in France, this bar adds a pop of color by the tub, lathers like a dream, and carries Frama's gorgeous Herbarium aroma that lingers on skin long after the shower.

Bleu de Chanel's Parfum takes everything great about the original and turns it up a notch. Still zesty and botanical, but with sandalwood and tonka bean lending a richer, smoother finish.

Released this year, Braun's Nevo is arguably the best and most advanced foil shaver on the market today, and our own testing backs that up. Given the price tag, it's exactly the sort of splurge that makes for a great gift.

Vitamins B and C do wonders for the skin, and Aesop's B Triple C Facial Balancing Gel is packed with both. Deeply hydrating yet leaving a matte finish, it was a game changer when it debuted over 20 years ago, and it's still elite after all these years.

If he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

Dior seems to drop a new olfactory banger every few months, and Bois d'Argent is one of the latest. Smooth woods, amber, and rich iris mingle with frankincense for a scent that's warm, elegant, and easy to wear just about anywhere.

Wonder Valley's newish Wild Garden hand wash puts olive oil to good use, whipping up a rich, softening lather with a cedar-and-herb scent that brings a little of the great outdoors to the sink.

A moisturizer is a no-brainer, but a serum signals one is getting extra serious about skincare. Caldera + Lab makes that addition easy: a few pumps deliver vitamin C, collagen amino acids, and skin-soothing botanicals to brighten, firm, and soften fine lines.

We've been longtime fans of Dr. Dennis Gross's Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel pads, which make good skincare almost embarrassingly easy. A couple of swipes help exfoliate dead skin, smooth texture, and brighten the complexion.

Tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

Salt & Stone makes one of our favorite body washes, and this mini set lets them take the whole lineup for a spin.

With these hydrating eye patches from one of the best grooming brands to do it, no one will ever know he didn't get his proper eight hours last night.

You can buy all the fancy sunscreen you want, but convenience decides if you actually wear it. Freaks of Nature’s SPF 50 stick—small, glide-on, reef safe, and water-resistant for 80 minutes—nails it.

The LED mask market is booming, and Omnilux is at the top of the heap. This one is specifically designed and FDA-cleared for men’s typically thicker facial skin, targeting fine lines, firmness, and overall health, while helping calm any redness from shaving. In other words, it’s a Michael Myers-like mask that promises scary-good skin with consistency and patience.

Hair dryers have officially gotten techy-cool, and Laifen is a big part of it. The new SE 2 is so sleek and ergonomic, with intuitive controls to match, he'll want to leave it on display.

Smythson and Burberry joining forces is more British heritage than you can wave a Union Jack at. Smythson already makes a covetable travel chess set, but add Burberry's signature check and it's, well, checkmate.

ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

It's a tabletop lighter shaped like a mallard duck. Something you'd find in the study of a delightfully eccentric uncle, and exactly the sort of gift no one knows they want until they get one.

A speckled enamelware thermos from Polo Country, because why not.

Few brands have done more to make everyday essentials like bedding, towels, and sleepwear into objects of desire than Copenhagen's Tekla. Its PJs embody that sensibility: beautifully cut, made from crisp organic cotton, and available in a killer assortment colors and stripes.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

If they're going to keep ordering pants off the internet, they might as well have a proper tool for opening all those packages. The Palmer knife makes short work of cardboard and packing tape, so they can get to the fit pics faster.

Hoto’s sleek PixelDrive electric screwdriver comes with 30 interchangeable bits and a nifty pixelated display that shows exactly how much power he’s working with. That wobbly dining chair doesn’t stand a chance.

This isn't one of those dinky makeup fridges. This is a countertop fridge fridge, the latest in beverage-holding innovation from Rocco. And of course, it looks great.

I picked up Nanu’s Arc earlier this year, and I’ve gotten way more joy out of it than I expected. It’s a well-built, thoughtfully engineered analog clock with a discreet digital display and a lovely mechanical chime. Not cheap, sure, but having one less reason to reach for my phone has been worth every penny.

Call me old-fashioned, but a man ought to know how to make a proper drink. And he ought to have the right tools for the job. Fellow's new eight-piece cocktail set has everything he needs to shake, stir, and strain his way to a good one.

It may come as a shock, but there's a whole world beyond burgers worth smashing. Caraway's immaculately designed grill press is up to the task.

A good set of bedsheets is a nice gift. An adult gift. It says, “I care about you, even when you're unconscious.” Parachute's brushed cotton sheets are those sheets: soft, cozy, and something they'll appreciate every single night.

Shinola's Michigan-made five-port power supply is a highly specific gift for the design obsessive in your life, but that's precisely why it'll hit.

Few things feel better than slipping into a plush robe at a fancy hotel, but honestly, most have nothing on Brooklinen's. Better yet, you don't need to spend $500 a night to get one.

Now that's one helluva coffee mug. Made from stainless steel with double-wall construction to keep it cool to the touch, this industrial number from Copenhagen-based design studio Service Projects comes with a generously proportioned saucer that does double duty as a serving tray.

John Waters warned against going home with someone who doesn't own books. I'd say the same rule goes for wine openers. And this one from Craighill really is the best.

You never know when you need a knife, pair of scissors, or a corkscrew—and now he'll never have to worry about missing any of those essential tools.

You could get him a candle. Or you could get him this handsome little contraption: a glass teardrop set in a brass cradle. Fill the glass with fragrance oil, light the tealight underneath, and voilà: instant home aura.

The most advanced vibe curators know: nothing sets the mood at home like well-crafted incense. Vyrao’s Verdant blend of bergamot, frankincense, and white musk packs a particularly calming punch as the seasons change.

Apple’s latest AirPods 3 refine a classic with noticeably better noise cancellation and a slick new live translation feature—proof the world’s best earbuds just keep getting smarter.

The new iPad mini gets its biggest glow-up yet, with a gorgeous 8.5-inch OLED display, the new A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter build that's now water-resistant.

Some folks are organized, the rest of us have AirTags. The second-generation model improves the range, cranks up the speaker volume, and generally makes losing things less stressful.

Apple's brand-new HomeView brings the company's signature polish to the smart home, giving them a sleek new command center for everything from lights to thermostats.

Plenty of brands have tried their hand at recreating Sony's classic Walkman headphones, and now Sony itself is getting in on the action. The MDR-3R brings back that familiar retro look, this time with a USB-C connection.

In our nostalgia-addled times, people are buying iPods again. Fosi Audio's DAP Neo takes the idea and brings it into the present, with a familiar form factor, tactile scroll wheel, and the ability to play high-resolution lossless audio. This bundle comes with the brand's excellent wired earbuds.

Ray-Ban’s Audio Clubmasters pack open-ear audio and six built-in microphones into a classic frame. Best of all, he can enjoy the latest tech without making everyone wonder if they’re being filmed.

The new Beats 360 headphones sound great and look the part. Swappable performance-knit cushions let you customize the look, while a sweat- and water-resistance rating makes them a rare pair of gym-worthy over-ears.

Amazon's Kindle Colorsoft makes a pretty convincing case for a color e-reader: admire the illustrations in a Taschen book, give comic books and graphic novels their due, or finally get around to reading The Creative Act. It does that, too.

We’ll always have a soft spot for a pen and spiral pad, but the Paper Pro Move is for the serious note taker—sleek, responsive, and slim enough to slip in a jacket pocket.

There's a newer Ace Ultra on the scene, but we're still big fans of the original Sonos Ace. The sound is rich and full, the battery lasts forever, and they have that luxe, comfortable-yet-minimalist feel you'd expect from one of the best home-audio brands, period.

Sometimes you just need a speaker small enough to toss in a tote for park hangs, solo listening sessions, or an impromptu dance party. Marshall's Emberton III is a great option.

Oura's fifth-gen ring is slimmer, lighter, and more comfortable than ever, with improved sensors for keeping tabs on sleep, recovery, and all the other things going on under the hood.

Aer's new Sports Duffel Max carries on the brand's tradition of making excellent gym bags, with plenty of room for a weekend warrior's gear and a clever pop-out divider that makes organizing equipment for just about any sport a snap.

Beat those sore muscles into submission so you can get back at it sooner rather than later.

Electrolytes have gotten awfully sophisticated lately. Freaks of Nature's zero-sugar powder goes beyond hydration, with a formula designed to support gut health and the skin barrier, too.

For the guy who can't start (or end) his day without getting a quick sweat sesh in, these shorts will keep him going rep after rep, set after set.

Calves barking after a vacation run? Worry no longer, thanks to these portable massage sleeves, which are great for those guys who never want to miss a run or a lift even if they're supposed to be taking time to rest.

You might think running requires little more than a pair of sneakers, but you'd be surprised. This vest from Lululemon has pockets aplenty for all the little things he needs to bring along, without weighing him down.

Give the guy an excuse to take a load off. Lookout & Wonderland’s Magic Bath combines mineral-rich Japanese sea salt, French green clay, and nourishing oils with 500 mg of CBD for a seriously luxurious soak.

#6471. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested—and retested—just about every meal delivery service. Each time we try HelloFresh, we’re impressed by its bold flavors, so we teamed up with the brand to bring you our favorite recipes each week (read more about how we chose them here). Sign up for a delivery, and you also get a 3-month digital subscription to BA for free. Here’s a closer look at one of our BA Picks.

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

#6470. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6469. Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

For 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’. It was plastered on the office walls and repeated ad nauseam by staff, but had no legal footing. Then, in 2021, creative directors Simeon Rose and Anne Hopkins put the provocation to a group of groundbreaking legal experts: how could they turn the slogan into something more?

Enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head. Some companies appoint a nature director — a human proxy for nature, who holds a formal board seat, written into the company’s articles of association, with the same financial and legal duties as other board members. Others appoint nature guardians, who perform a similar role in advocating for nature at the board level, but they don’t necessarily have voting rights.

A new programme by Kering and the Centre for Sustainable Fashion hopes to reimagine how companies make high-level decisions, but is the industry ready to embrace change?

NOTB was proposed by Faith In Nature, and fleshed out by legal non-profits Lawyers for Nature and the Earth Law Center (ELC), but it was inspired by Indigenous communities who have practiced nature-centric governance for millennia. “The current business system is operating exactly as it was designed to: businesses pool capital, build goods and services at scale, speed and low cost, and accrue benefits for shareholders,” explains Mary Johnstone-Louis, senior fellow in management at the University of Oxford’s Saïd Business School. “Putting nature on the board is radical because it introduces a stakeholder on which every business depends, but whose interests are not typically represented at the board level.”

While there was no precedent for putting nature on the board, there were other case studies to draw on, says Lawyers for Nature co-founder and managing director Brontie Ansell. “Until relatively recently, women were seen as objects of law, rather than subjects of law. Like nature, they were not allowed to hold property, vote or voice concerns. Now, we look back on that with horror,” she explains. “Likewise, we are very familiar with widening the stakeholder pool in boardrooms. Many now include HR managers, union representatives, and health and safety officers. Extending this to nature is critical to human survival.”

Alongside Faith In Nature, NOTB has since been adopted by dozens of companies, including British interiors brand House of Hackney, Norwegian apparel brand Northern Playground, and French IT services company Norsys. Each has put their own spin on the blueprint, contributing to a fast-evolving consensus on best practices, and throwing open the doors for further innovation. Vogue Business invited these early adopters to share the tensions, toggles and opportunities.

Businesses are just as diverse and idiosyncratic as nature, says Faith In Nature managing director Hannah Whittaker. When it comes to putting nature on the board, each business has to do it in its own way.

NOTB encourages companies to give nature voting rights, but it’s possible to test nature governance without this. Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia made waves in 2022 when it created a nature purpose trust model, making a collection of environmental non-profits the beneficiary of 98% of its non-voting stock, while retaining approval rights in the Patagonia Purpose Trust, controlled by the family of founder Yvon Chouinard.

Approaches may also differ by jurisdiction, notes ELC’s nature governance business development associate Anna Solgaard, who acts as the nature guardian for Norwegian clothing label Northern Playground. Finding ways to give nature more legal rights requires “creative lawyering”, adds Alexandra Pimor, director of the ELC’s Nature Governance Agency. “That’s the beauty of nature on the board: we did not have to change the law to do it, we just changed our relationship with the law to give it a different purpose [taking existing rights for board members and extending them to nature]. In a capitalist environment, the corporate world is probably the easiest place to embed the voice of nature, because companies are given so much freedom.”

At Norsys, nature is both a director and a shareholder with a 10% stake in the business. “This is a strong model because it means nature will always be represented on the board, it’s not just one nomination we forget about in three years,” says the company’s nature director Frantz Gault, author of Nature at Work and co-founder of Vivøices, a public interest organization promoting the representation of the living world in organizational governance. Gault helped design the nature governance at Norsys, complementing his own role with a council of advisors, who also decide how dividends from nature’s 10% stake are spent.

Lawyers for Nature, on the other hand, prefers for nature directors to remain as “conflict-free” as possible. In the frameworks it has designed, nature representatives are not heavily salaried by the company, they don’t have a bonus linked to profit, they don’t owe the company money or vice versa, and they don’t have — or at least, they commit to disclosing — any other conflicts of interest. “By minimizing those conflicts, the nature representative can speak in the purest form possible about what nature needs,” says Ansell.

At Northern Playground, the articles of association include a “safety valve” whereby the nature proxy can be relieved of their duties if the company is approaching bankruptcy, to reduce the risk of them being held personally liable.

Another contention point is whether the nature proxy should have the right to veto strategic decisions, as well as voting on them. “If you get to the point where you need a veto, you’ve already lost,” says Dr Juliet Rose, head of development at the British botanical garden and research hub The Eden Project, and nature director at Faith In Nature. “You’re trying to get everybody moving in the same direction, so nobody even suggests something that would require a veto.”

At Norsys, Gault has the power to veto, but has never activated it. To keep the “nuclear power” in check, he is required to confer with a council of 10 scientific experts before taking a position in board meetings. Still, knowing the veto exists can be persuasive enough. “Everyone knows I have the power to veto, so the other directors listen when I speak, and they work with me to find a consensus.” If a veto isn’t on the cards, companies can implement the right to disagree, and the right to express that disagreement in public, adds Gault, or the right to resign. “These are little legal technicalities, but they help make nature’s voice more meaningful.”

Whichever approach a company chooses, Vivøices recommends running a year-long pilot before codifying nature’s role or communicating the program to consumers. “You do a pilot, then map the impact and what happened, how it changed the way decisions were made, how it influenced the culture internally, and what it means to really integrate the position of nature,” says co-founder Niels de Fraguier.

When House of Hackney advertised a directorship “for mother nature and future generations” in 2023, it received over 500 applications — its most popular job listing to date. But finding the right person to represent something as nebulous as nature was no small feat. “We had applications from scientists, teachers, poets and everything in between,” says House of Hackney co-founder Frieda Gormley, author of In the Company of Nature.

The challenge is finding someone who can bridge economic and ecological realities, says the University of Oxford’s Johnstone-Louis. “They have to protect the company, and at the same time, they have to speak for nature. That means they have to toggle between immediacy and long-termism; between business as usual and what business could be,” she says. Regardless of their professional background, humility and diplomacy are the key competencies, adds de Fraguier.

Both Faith In Nature and House of Hackney appointed Lawyers for Nature’s Ansell as their inaugural nature director, establishing the legal basis for the role and ironing out any kinks. Her successors have wildly different skill sets: Rose has a background in plant science and ecology, while House of Hackney’s nature director Charmian Love specializes in governance, having co-founded B Lab UK, the organization behind the B Corp certification. Love says her goal is to create tools that make it easier for more diverse nature proxies to step into the role in future, while Rose says her success is defined by how well she empowers staff throughout the company, so whoever holds the nature directorship is not working alone, or resting solely on their own, inevitably limited, experience.

Ideally, nature-centric decision-making cascades down through the company, and the nature director works in tandem with a well-established nature lead. While the former stewards the long-term purpose of the business, the latter embeds it in day-to-day operations. Without a nature director in their corner, a nature lead can easily fall into the same trap as sustainability leads, tasked with overhauling the business but lacking the resource or buy-in to do so, instead operating in a silo and trying to shoehorn change into business as usual. And without a nature lead to operationalize nature-centric decision-making, a nature director risks becoming little more than “window dressing”, says Johnstone-Louis.

To avoid tokenizing nature, Faith In Nature has designed a nature dashboard, which translates its goals into tangible projects each team can track progress against. Projects fall into five governing principles: governance, operational impact, sourcing, community and regeneration. “We had to work through the confusion and connect each team with the outcomes we wanted for nature, each of which has budgets, resources and KPIs attached,” explains Whittaker. “Otherwise, the concept can be quite theoretical for staff.” These projects span from changing the adhesive on labels to make at-home recycling easier, to running the brand’s first major television ad in collaboration with Channel 4 and B Corp.

At House of Hackney, Love starts every board meeting with a nature degradation pulse-check and a poem about nature, based on climate policy leader Nigel Topping’s remarks that “we need to be guided by science and moved by poetry”. Beyond board meetings, Love has defined 10 topics that are material to nature, from supply chain and procurement to regulatory changes and financial investments. Decisions about these topics are automatically escalated to a monthly nature meeting. She has also introduced a spin on the traditional ‘going concern test’ boards use to assess how nature-related decisions will affect the company’s future viability and license to operate.

On top of this, Love has a private email address where staff can discreetly voice concerns or ideas, and the company regularly invites inspirational nature-related speakers into the office. The next phase is to trial a physical card game, she says, which will live in every meeting room, encouraging staff to question their daily decision-making through a nature-centric lens, inspired by similar games at tea brand Pukka Herbs. And at the end of the year, House of Hackney will publish an open-source toolkit for NOTB, informed by its Greenprint fellowship, where 10 SMEs — including Lush, Davines and Vivobarefoot — experimented with nature governance over 12 months.

NOTB is not just another sustainability box for companies to tick; it’s a paradigm shift that goes beyond sustainability, toward regeneration.

“Philosophically, these are two very different landscapes,” explains Solgaard. “Sustainability is an anthropocentric paradigm, but nature is ecocentric, which means that the more-than-human world is valued alongside humans. Sustainability works with separation and reductionism, which is why we have all these boxes to tick, and we struggle to view things holistically, or to see how everything is interconnected. Nature is everything.”

Putting nature on the board also means moving beyond the risk mitigation approach that has defined so many corporate nature strategies, and underscored the business case for nature, to date, adds Johnstone-Louis. The risk mitigation approach asks how companies can continue to extract resources like cotton and wool pulp from nature, and reduce supply chain disruption from nature-related disasters like water scarcity and flooding. The NOTB approach — especially for companies like House of Hackney, which have combined nature with future generations — asks how decisions made today will affect the ability of future systems to thrive, sometimes looking as far ahead as seven generations. “It’s a different way of seeing the world,” she adds.

Addressing nature directly is a leap into the unknown — not least because so few companies have mapped their nature risks and dependencies. But rather than face this with fear, Pimor encourages companies to see the opportunities. “We are facing the most incredible, unprecedented ecological challenge. Facing the unknown means becoming more open to creativity, innovation and imagination. That’s what the voice of nature brings to the table.”

Deep transformation tends to be slow and steady, concludes Ansell. “Slow isn’t ideal in the situation we find ourselves in, but it’s better than going backwards. The idea here is for nature to be a gentle guiding voice, moving the rudder one degree at a time until the ship has completely changed course. It’s exciting. There’s so much still up for grabs in terms of distilling the theory and making it work for each individual sector or situation.”

#6467. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman says. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

The holidays are upon us, and with them come feasts in many forms. Maybe you’re looking forward to a traditional Thanksgiving dinner with all the fixings or can’t wait to eat so many latkes that you reach food-coma status. When it comes to dressing for the end-of-year celebrations, many focus on looking festive when, perhaps, we should emphasize just as much comfort.

With so many food-centric holidays in the immediate future, the Vogue staff is preparing to enjoy many a meal without sacrificing fashion. Enter the eating pants. When planning an outfit around the activity of breaking bread, our team favors everything from the ultra-high-waist to low-slung, denim to silk.

So whether your holiday and Thanksgiving dress codes lean formal or casual, Vogue has got you covered. Below, check out the staff’s picks for the best eating pants to enjoy your meal and your outfit.

Not only the perfect satin shade of cranberry sauce but a waistband that allows for all the stuffing! —Chloe Malle, head of editorial content

Elasticized waist, roomy pockets, the chic pleats! In dark red these Issey Miyake Pleats Please pants are perfect not just for Thanksgiving, but for the whole holiday season. —Nicole Phelps, global fashion features director

I like that these pants come in that popular barrel-shaped cut, which feels very relaxed and easy, but the wool makes it feel just a tad dressy. But of course it’s the forgiving elastic waistband that’s the real draw…I WILL be having a second slice of pumpkin pie, thankyouverymuch. —Max Berlinger, senior fashion news editor

For holidays filled with indulgent meals with those you love most, dressing appropriately is a top priority. I like to choose silk pants with an elastic waistband for comfort and a polished look. I love their versatility; these Comme Si trousers can be dressed up with a billowy blouse or button-down, or dressed down with a tee and a cozy knit. —Andrea Zendejas, commerce market editor

With a front pleat and a kick flare, no one will even notice that you’ve snuck an imposter into the formal dinner pant rotation. —Alexandra Hildreth, fashion news writer

I absolutely loathe a waistband squeezing my stomach when I’m trying to enjoy a meal, so I’m partial to a pair of low-slung pants. I find that Levi’s 501s ’90s Jeans sit perfectly on my hips and leave plenty of room to eat. I recommend sizing up to exaggerate the baggy look. —Hannah Jackson, senior fashion writer

This year I really got into the balloon pants trend, and these black Suzie Kondi trousers so happen to be the perfect Thanksgiving eating pants, given they have an elastic waist and roomy, non-restrictive silhouette. —Christian Allaire, senior fashion and style writer

Baggy jeans are my go-to. I love EB Denim’s low-rise baggy jeans, which are my daily uniform anyway. This year, though, I’m leaning more even cozy with a pair of cashmere pants. As a non-American, I don’t technically celebrate Thanksgiving, but it feels as good an excuse as any to pull out a pair of soft but chic trousers for a day spent lounging around. These from Noname Is Needed look like a good option. (The brand is from the same team as Naked Cashmere, so it’s a safe bet.) —Madeleine Schulz, reporter, Vogue Business

Universal Standard leggings. I’ve had mine for six years, and they’re flawless and can accommodate a full Thanksgiving meal. —Emma Specter, culture writer

During Thanksgiving, I love to try all the foods but not feel constricted or uncomfortable with my clothing. I like to wear something that still looks put-together and not too casual, while secretly allowing for comfort. Ideally, I’d wear a nice tailored pant like these Aflalo Danika trouser that have a nice looseness to them.

I also love the Leset Barb silk pants, or the Deiji Studios Ease trouser, which both have secret elastic waistbands, but still look chic. No unbuttoning needed. —Dayla Benor, senior commerce writer, Vogue Shopping

I always change into pajama pants at some point during my Thanksgiving dinner, so this year I might as well wear pajama pants from the get-go. I love all the loungewear pieces from Comme Si. (Everyone is wearing it, including NewJeans, my favorite style icons.) The green-striped pair with a knit and some Uggs sounds extra cozy for Thanksgiving...although my parents might yell at me for dressing too comfortably. —Irene Kim, production and editorial coordinator, Vogue Runway

#6465. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6463. “Focus on Learning”: Career Lessons With Burberry’s Daniel Lee and Anna Wintour

The morning after Vogue World 2026: Milano, all anyone online wanted to talk about was “the robots”. The moment became a lightning rod for memes, TikTok reactions, and questions about the state of creativity today. It turns out that was sort of the point.

A couple of months after the event, Anna Wintour, chief content officer at Condé Nast and global editorial director of Vogue, invited Burberry’s chief creative officer Daniel Lee to New York for a fireside chat at the Vogue Business Global Summit. Lee also wanted to talk about “the robots”.

A robot walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026.

Of course, the two discussed much more than that, taking turns interviewing each other about Lee’s journey at the British brand during a company-wide turnaround, Wintour’s first job in fashion, the US midterms that happened the day before, and success — spoiler: social media makes it look easy. Ahead of the official announcement, Wintour also teased the Met Costume Institute’s theme for 2027: extraORDINARY.

Anna Wintour: Daniel, good morning. Thank you for coming all the way from London. So Daniel, you chose a very quiet news day here in the US. Have you been following the election news?

Daniel Lee: Yeah, definitely. I was super jet-lagged, so I was watching the news all night.

AW: I have to ask you, how do you think [Senator-elect] James Talarico would look in a Burberry suit?

DL: Well, I’d be happy to see anyone looking great in a Burberry suit.

Anna and Daniel on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit.

AW: Very diplomatic. I guess you’re a Burberry ambassador. I read that you first thought you wanted to be a designer when your aunt took you to see the windows at Harvey Nichols in Leeds as a boy. I guess the equivalent over here would be Saks. Do you agree?

DL: Yes, I’m afraid that is true. You know, I didn’t fall into fashion by looking through pages of Vogue. That’s probably the story I should start saying. I mean, I grew up in the north of England in an area called Yorkshire, which is very beautiful — it’s in the countryside and very green. It rains a lot.

DL: David Hockney is from my hometown. Also, Christopher Bailey is from the same area [Yorkshire]. The Burberry trench coats are made in that area, so I guess Burberry was somehow ingrained in me since I was born. Clothes were really practical in my childhood. Fashion wasn’t something that was really part of my family or my upbringing. We wore clothes to stay warm and dry.

DL: Very Burberry. As kids, we liked to play outside. We would spend our childhood riding bikes in the rain, in Wellington boots. When Harvey Nichols opened in Leeds, I remember going past that store and seeing these incredible windows, and I guess I realized clothes could be so much more. It was like seeing a fantasyland. I guess that’s when I started to think this maybe could be a career for me.

DL: Eventually, yes. As a child, I think my first instinct was to get out of Yorkshire. As much as I love the countryside, I knew there was more. I was curious.

AW: Well, you did just buy a house there, so you must like it?

DL: You stay connected to your roots. But I think, as a 12-year-old, I went to London for the first time, and I remember seeing the variety of people in the streets, seeing the theater, so many things going on. I really wanted to be part of that culture. I think that’s what initially drew me to London and eventually to art school. I went to [Central] Saint Martins. I did an art foundation year, into fashion qualifications later on.

AW: OK. You’re meant to ask me a question now.

DL: Anna, what was your first job in fashion? And what did you learn from it?

AW: I’m going to talk about the first job that I actually enjoyed in fashion, which was working at Harper’s & Queen (now Harper’s Bazaar UK) in London, where there were two to three people — on a good day — in the fashion department. So I went in there, and I was immediately an editor, even though I had zero experience. I was always so very grateful for that training because there were no budgets. I do remember my boss once giving me maybe £10 or £20 and saying, ‘Anna, go to Morocco or go south. Find a sheikh, find a maharaja, and do a shoot.’ And somehow you did. It was just a different attitude. You had to be so creative and make things out of nothing. Because there were no teams at Harper’s & Queen, I learned how to do everything: you covered the market, you did the shoots, you wrote the captions.

When I came to New York, I went to work at Harper’s Bazaar [US]. I got fired fairly immediately because they told me I would never understand the American market, which is probably true. I then landed on my feet at New York Magazine, which was unbelievable training because I was working in a newsroom with guys like Nick Pileggi and Tom Wolfe — all the great writers of that time. They didn’t give a damn about what I did. They put me next to the bathrooms, so I got to see everybody coming in and out. Because nobody cared about fashion or style, they just left me alone. Eventually, I got a call from Condé Nast. It’s interesting when you talk to young people today how they’re focused on success, and they’re not focused on learning. Without the base, you can't succeed.

I’m meant to ask you a question now. So, congratulations on your very successful show in September. I think it was the first time you collaborated with anyone creatively, and the person that you chose to collaborate with is Celia Birtwell — she’s an 85-year-old legend in textile design, a partner to the great Ossie Clark. Did you have to do much convincing to get her involved? Maybe explain to our audience a little bit more about who she is.

DL: I would say Celia is probably mostly known as Ossie Clark’s collaborator in all those years of incredible dresses and work that I think is on every designer’s moodboard. And she was also very, very close friends with David Hockney and is a subject in many beautiful pieces of his work. We were celebrating 170 years of Burberry this year. We wanted to do the brand justice, and we were thinking of ways to do new things. I met with Celia, actually, just for a conversation. You never really know if someone’s going to be interested in working together. People are terrified by our timelines.

Textile designer Celia Birtwell with her partner and collaborator Ossie Clark in July 1971. Birtwell’s prints for Clark’s dresses are, in Daniel Lee’s words, “on every designer's moodboard.”

She came to the meeting saying, ‘You know, I’m really inspired by the check. I love the way Hockney paints ginghams on a tablecloth, the perspective that he gives to that.’ I said, ‘Well, would you be up for making some new work?’ And she did. She started with the checks, then the ginghams, and then the beautiful kind of English florals. Hockney gives me so much joy, emotion and warmth.

Birtwell’s new take on the brand’s check was inspired by the way David Hockney paints gingham on a tablecloth.

AW: Yeah, and he was so prolific, painting right up until the end, using an iPad, using different ways to make art. I’m sure you saw that last incredible show that was on at the Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris. What a life. [Now] you’re meant to ask me…

DL: Congratulations on Vogue World: Milan. Would you like to talk about the robots?

AW: I’d love to. So the subject of Vogue World: Milan was our belief in the art of the human hand, the creativity of the hand, and the human mind in the age of technology. And we felt that to add something that represented technology, in a way that was — in my view — faintly ridiculous, reinforced the idea behind the theme of the exhibition. As is often in my case, not everyone agreed with me, but it certainly caused a lot of conversation.

Gigi Hadid at Vogue World: Milano. The show celebrated, in Anna Wintour’s words, “the art of the human hand” in the age of technology.

We’re moving on now to San Francisco in September, and we’re really going to be addressing the diversity and the incredible communities that live in San Francisco, and how it’s a city that has stood up for so much. The symphony and the museums there are extraordinary.

Talking about San Francisco, let’s talk about tech. Your last collection seemed to us that you were really advocating the celebration of imperfection and the romance of things made by hand. Is that true? And what do you feel about AI in terms of your creative work?

DL: As a child, I would spend my time making birthday cards, making cakes with my mom and making dance costumes for my sister. I’m a maker. Obviously I have a mobile phone, but tech is not a huge part of my life per se. I’m not a big computer gamer; I never even check email. I only really use WhatsApp.

DL: I think that’s what I love about luxury fashion. I really think luxury is about preservation of this savoir-faire, this craftsmanship. One of the main roles of the creative directors and companies today is to preserve that know-how and make it relevant, so that customers today can appreciate it.

OK, Anna, could you tell us more about next year’s Costume Institute show?

AW: Absolutely. It’s going to be extraordinary.

Daniel, I think it’s five years that you’ve been at Burberry?

AW: You went into a company that was in disarray, and looking at it from the outside, maybe not very well run. Two years ago, CEO Joshua Schulman came in. That must have been very welcome to have a good partner. He’s been integral — led by your creativity — to Burberry’s unbelievable turnaround. What is it like to work with Josh?

DL: Josh brought an incredible energy, passion, and belief in Burberry. He loves the brand, and his energy really reverberates in the company. I think that’s the role of a great leader. Josh brought a lot of discipline to the brand. He really grew up in American department stores; he intimately understands wholesalers and has very personal relationships with them.

Daniel Lee, Anna Wintour and Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman. Lee credits Schulman, who joined two years ago, with bringing “discipline” and a clear pricing strategy to the brand’s turnaround.

AW: I remember being in your store on a Saturday morning looking for something for a small child, and he was there, folding the scarves.

DL: We laugh, but Josh spends his vacations in malls. We had an executive dinner and were asked about our favorite places, and I’m sure he mentioned a mall in California. When he arrived, he brought a very clear idea around price architecture.

Anna, what do you think the British fashion industry needs at the moment?

AW: I think they need to really focus on who they are. We all look to London for creativity and individuality — and a degree of eccentricity. There’s a freedom to the way you see the kids dressed in the streets there that is the antithesis of American or cool Italian, more luxury dressing. It’s a little bit closer to what I was saying when I first was working in London, when you had to do everything.

I think that the British Fashion Council really needs to focus on that and make more noise about what you can see in London that you cannot see anywhere else. They have a great brand like Burberry, and it was so wonderful to see McQueen back in London and Christopher Kane at Mulberry.

They have so many creative kids, students, who can’t get jobs there, so they need to make sure that London becomes more of a global fashion mecca — that the retailers, the CEOs, and the journalists go. [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham seems like he’s going to be much more open to business in the UK, and they need to lean on what they own.

Burberry Spring/Summer 2027, a collection that celebrates handcraft and the brand’s 170th year.

So, the last shows were followed by quite a few creative director departures and appointments. How do you see this constant creative shuffle shaping the industry?

DL: My experience is that it takes time to understand and have a dialogue with the company that you work for, understand the archive, the culture, the people. It also takes time to build a team, and people need stability. I advocate for continuity. Also, when there are constant aesthetic shifts, it’s hard for the customer to understand that. I think there are moments where things do need to be revolutionized, and change is needed. Change is good. But too much change is discombobulating. It’s incredibly hard when you join a brand.

What do you think is the future of what we used to call magazines?

AW: I was doing an interview with Grace Coddington, who’s worked at Vogue for so many years, and we were reminiscing about when we were only working on print. She was able to go off to these extraordinary locations for what seems like an unthinkable amount of time — probably only with £20 in her pocket. She would go to Scotland for 10 days; she would go to China for two weeks. There was a great luxury in being able to have time to plan and think about what an issue of Vogue should look like. But it was a very narrow audience. When I first arrived at Vogue, people would disappear in the afternoons because they were going to Jones Beach — there just wasn’t that much to do.

Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington. Recalling their print days, Wintour remembers when Coddington could spend 10 days shooting in Scotland or two weeks in China. That was “a great luxury,” she says, but for a much narrower audience.

How lucky are we now to have all these amazing platforms to talk to our audiences? Our audiences have grown to unthinkable numbers. One of the great experiences and joys of what I do now is helping Adam [Baidawi, GQ’s global editorial director], Chloe [Malle, American Vogue’s head of editorial content], and Chioma [Nnadi, British Vogue’s head of editorial content], and all the editors that I work with over the world.

This afternoon, I’m leaving for Asia to work with our editors in Japan, China, Taiwan, and beyond. And I learn a lot from all of them. You have to be on the ground. I really feel that it’s so important to understand different cultures and how they think and work. I remember years and years ago, when I was first starting out, a great friend of mine said, ‘Anna, wherever you are, you have to walk in the street, climb a high point, visit a museum, and have a cup of coffee.’ I always remember that. I think sometimes when people get successful, they don’t walk in the street. When you walk in the street, that’s when you see the world.

What advice do you give those who want to become creative directors? Do you think social media has distorted the way young creatives see their trajectory by making them think they can be their own boss, or do you think it’s a good thing?

DL: I think social media makes things look very easy. People don’t always see the journey: the highs, the lows, the learnings. I don’t think you should set out to be an overnight success or to have instant gratification on social media. I’ve been every level, every part of a studio. I’ve been the intern, the pattern maker, the design director. I’ve lived all those jobs, and I’ve had those experiences, and that helps me do the job I do today.

AW: This is an audience of mostly executives. What’s one piece of advice you would give to them when it comes to working with creative teams?

DL: I think empathy is very important, respect is very important, understanding is important, and humility. No one’s right all the time. My favorite kind of working relationship is when it feels collaborative. I think as a creative leader, I try to create a space and framework to allow people to feel safe. I think this is something I once heard you say: ‘You hire great people, and you let them work.’ Trust is important.

#6462. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.
